role: Sorter at an herbal tea factory
headline: Off to an electronics factory in Xiamen at eighteen, home for six years raising children, and only once the youngest started primary school taken on at an herbal tea factory on her doorstep in Longhai, Zhangzhou: a sorter who picks over chrysanthemum buds one by one at a stainless steel table every day, to the clack of the tea-bag packing machine
unit: An herbal tea processing factory in Longhai, Zhangzhou, Fujian (packing pyramid tea bags for a dozen online wellness tea brands, and making the raw herbs for southern Fujian's green-herb tea; two workshops, about eighty people)
level: The electronics factory trained you to quick hands and sharp eyes, and you can sit still for hours. You can't yet tell good from bad in chrysanthemum buds, roses or cassia seeds, and you can't run a single machine
intro: Your younger one has started first grade. You see him in at the school gate, and ten minutes on the e-bike gets you to the factory gate. HR gives you a blue cap, a face mask and a pair of white rubber shoes, takes you through the air shower and leads you to a stainless steel sorting table spread with a layer of golden chrysanthemum buds. As of today, in the wellness teas a dozen online brands sell, some of the flowers have been picked over one by one by you.
salary_note: Estimate: at a food contract factory in Zhangzhou, line workers get base pay plus a piece rate, with plenty of overtime in peak season (Singles' Day, the New Year shopping festival), taking home a notch below the national figure. As a workshop director or production manager, the pay is upper-middle for local small and mid-sized food factories.

facts.label: Next level up
facts.value: Herbal Tea Processing Worker, Level 4 (Machine Operator) (1-3 years)

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Picking out impurities and moldy material from the raw herbs

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: You warm milk and steamed buns for the two children and tie the elder one's red scarf. Your mother-in-law calls from the yard for you to go, she'll take them.

At the factory you change into your uniform, tuck all your hair into the cap, mask, gloves, white rubber shoes. You step into the air shower; the wind blasts from all four sides, and you count to ten with your eyes shut.

The pre-shift meeting. The team leader reads out today's orders: twenty thousand bags of red bean and job's tears tea for an online brand, ten thousand of chrysanthemum and cassia seed, and this afternoon a batch of green-herb tea material to dry.

The sorting table. A crate of chrysanthemum buds tipped onto the tabletop, and you and the women opposite pick over them heads down: the ones gone black at the heart, the ones with insect holes, stray bits of stalk, plucked out one by one into the bowl beside you. They chat in Minnan about last night's TV drama, their hands never stopping.
Next door the roaster starts on the red beans and job's tears, and the whole workshop fills with a toasty smell. The machine operator grabs a handful, bites one and says two more minutes.
The canteen: one meat dish, two vegetables and a bowl of soup. Afterwards in the changing room you phone your mother-in-law to ask whether the little one cried this morning.

In the afternoon you're moved to boxing beside the pyramid tea-bag machine. It clacks out bag after bag, and every half hour you pull ten to weigh. One is half a gram light, and you take it to the operator.

Clocking off. You ride the e-bike past a grove of longan trees and buy a bunch of greens at a roadside stall. At home the elder one is doing homework, and your husband video-calls from Xiamen to say he's coming back this weekend.

ladder.title: Sorting Worker
ladder.focus: Sort raw material, pick out impurities, box, label and clean the workshop, paid by the piece. You get to learn a machine on quick hands, clean sorting and no mistakes.

ladder.title: Herbal Tea Processing Worker, Level 4 (Machine Operator)
ladder.focus: Run a dryer, roaster, cutter or pyramid tea-bag packer on your own: set temperature and time to the process sheet, change materials, clear jams, spot-check weights and seals. You move up on steady output and little downtime.

ladder.title: Team Leader
ladder.focus: Lead a shift of a dozen people: assign posts, run handovers, track each order's progress and spot checks, handle ordinary quality problems, train newcomers. You move up on your team's output, pass rate and keeping people.

ladder.title: Workshop Director
ladder.focus: Run one workshop's schedule, staff, equipment and hygiene, host brands' factory audits and handle complaints, and settle raw materials with quality control and purchasing. You move up on delivery dates, pass rates and audit scores.

ladder.title: Production Manager
ladder.focus: Run the whole factory's production plan, new product samples, equipment purchases and compliance with the food production license, and negotiate capacity and delivery with the owner and the brands. You hold the job on the factory's capacity, quality and costs.

ai_tasks.name: Picking out impurities and moldy material from the raw herbs
ai_tasks.how: AI vision sorters can spot and reject obvious impurities and moldy pieces. People deal with material that looks alike or smells wrong, and regularly recalibrate the standard.

ai_tasks.name: Washing the raw material and draining it
ai_tasks.how: Washing and draining can be done by an automated washing line to a set program. A person only spot-checks how clean it is and how the equipment is running.

ai_tasks.name: Cutting, crushing or grinding the raw material to the process spec
ai_tasks.how: Machines cut and grind to set specs, and AI can help tune the parameters. People adjust blades and particle size to how dry, fibrous or tender the material is, and deal with jams.

ai_tasks.name: Running the de-enzyming, drying and other equipment to dry the raw material
ai_tasks.how: Smart control systems can run the de-enzyming and drying curves automatically and monitor temperature and humidity. A person has to judge whether the material is done, and step in when batches differ.

ai_tasks.name: Controlling processing temperature and time, and adjusting the forming process
ai_tasks.how: AI can recommend temperature and time combinations from sensor data. People set the final process by judging the finished product's taste and color, and answer for the result.

ai_tasks.name: Blending ingredients to the recipe ratio
ai_tasks.how: The system can calculate and weigh the ingredients to the recipe automatically. People confirm batch differences in the raw material, fine-tune the ratio and check the finished flavor.

ai_tasks.name: Packing, sealing and labeling the finished product
ai_tasks.how: Automatic packing lines can weigh, bag, seal, label and print codes. A person only changes materials, troubleshoots and spot-checks packing quality.

ai_tasks.name: Spot-checking products for sensory quality, moisture and hygiene
ai_tasks.how: Inline instruments and AI can test moisture and other indicators automatically and log the data. People do the sensory evaluation, keep sampling to spec, rule on anomalies and give final release.

events.e_yellow_fingers: After a week of sorting chrysanthemum, the dirt under your nails is all yellow and won't wash out. Your elder child takes your hand and asks if you're ill. It's the color of the flowers, you say.
events.e_fast_hands: When the month's piece-rate figures came out, you'd sorted the most at the table. The woman opposite said anyone could tell you'd trained in a Xiamen factory: your hands are faster than your eyes.
events.e_kid_fever: Your younger one ran a fever in the night, and you sat holding him at the township clinic until dawn, then took the morning off and lost that month's perfect-attendance bonus. The team leader said phone ahead next time, and she can help you swap shifts.
events.e_sorter: The factory bought an optical sorter: material pours down through it and the wrong-colored pieces are blown away in an instant. The sorting table went from twelve people to five, and you were kept on to pick out only the kinds the machine can't tell apart.
events.e_live: An influencer sold the red bean and job's tears tea your factory makes in a livestream, over a hundred thousand orders in one night. The factory ran overtime five days straight; when you got home the children were asleep, and on the table was a bowl of thin noodles your mother-in-law had cooked.
events.e_metal: The metal detector on the packing line went off: a bag with a short piece of fine wire in it. The whole batch of twenty thousand bags was stopped and run through the machine again, and a few of you searched until midnight, finally finding it came from the stitching on a raw-material sack.
events.e_mold: In the damp of the spring "return south" weather, a batch of rosebuds in the warehouse got damp and grew spots of mold. You and quality control opened sack after sack, smelling and looking flower by flower, and the sacks with mold were scrapped whole. Lucky it never reached the packing line, quality control said.
events.e_husband: Your husband quit his work in Xiamen and came back to Longhai to drive a truck, sometimes hauling for your factory. The first time he delivered raw material, he waited at the gate for you to finish, and told the guard he was family.
events.e_contest: The factory held a skills competition: who could sort the most, the cleanest, in twenty minutes. You came first, and the prize was a rice cooker. You carried it home, and your mother-in-law used it to make a pot of taro rice.
events.e_burn: Cleaning the roaster before the drum had cooled, your wrist touched it and rose in a blister. The operator said even switched off that thing needs half an hour, and you remembered.
events.e_auto_pack: The packing workshop got a new line that weighs, bags, seals, labels and prints codes in one go, with robot arms doing the boxing. Work that took ten people now takes three watching, and the rest were moved to other workshops.
events.e_audit: A big brand came to audit the factory, the auditor running white-gloved fingers into the corners of the machines and leafing through every production record. Your machine's checklist was missing a signature for one day, and it went on the report. The team leader didn't say anything to you, but you felt bad about it for days.
events.e_qingcao: The factory couldn't get enough green-herb tea material, and the owner asked old people from the village to go up the hill and pick. You went along once, and an old woman taught you to know beggarticks, plantain and fish mint, saying the bitter bowl of cooling tea you drank as a child was boiled from these.
events.e_mother_in_law: Your mother-in-law had a fall and went into hospital, and there was no one to collect the children. You swapped onto the early shift with the team leader, clocking off at three to collect them and going to the hospital in the evening.
events.e_complaint: A brand passed on a complaint: a customer said they'd found a hair in a tea bag, with a photo. You took your team through that day's security footage, changing-room logs and air-shower records line by line, and at the meeting afterwards you went over the rules on caps once more.
events.e_house: You put down a deposit on a flat in central Longhai, since the elder one will go to middle school in town. On moving day you wrapped the factory rice cooker in three layers of newspaper.
events.e_new_recipe: A brand wanted a new mulberry leaf and corn silk tea, and the samples went through eleven versions. In the sample room you blended, brewed and tasted version after version, and at the eleventh the owner took a sip and said: this one.
events.e_apprentice: The new girl, just out of vocational school, kept forgetting to stop the packing machine before changing material. You didn't scold her; you walked her through starting, changing and stopping twenty times, until she could do it with her eyes shut.
events.e_legs: On your feet in the workshop all day, the veins in your calves have risen one by one, and your legs cramp in your sleep at night. The doctor told you to wear compression stockings, and you bought three pairs online, from a shop selling the free gifts that came with a wellness tea brand your factory packs for.
events.e_kid_college: Your elder child got into a university in Fuzhou. On the day you took him to register, you tucked a few packs of the factory's chrysanthemum tea into his suitcase and told him to make one when he stays up late.
events.e_dashboard: The factory installed a production system, and every machine's output, downtime and pass rate jumps across a big screen. You no longer leaf through paper reports at the morning meeting; you point at the screen and say which machine stopped for forty minutes yesterday.
events.e_eyes: You find you have to bring your eyes very close to sort chrysanthemum now. You got a pair of reading glasses and hung them by the sorting table, and the young newcomers sometimes borrow them to try on for fun.

c_machine.title: Learn to run a machine or not
c_machine.situation: The operator of the packing machine is going on maternity leave, and the team leader asks if you want to learn the pyramid tea-bag packer. Once you know it, it's ¥800 more a month, but the sorting piece rate is gone, and when the machine goes wrong it's on you; at the sorting table you already sort more than anyone.

options.label: Learn the machine
options.result: You learned from the operator for two weeks: changing the film roll, setting the weighing, clearing jams. The day she left, the machine didn't spoil a single bag in your hands.

options.label: Stay at the sorting table
options.result: You said you'd sort a while longer. At the end of the month you still topped the piece rate, and the woman opposite called you the anchor of the sorting table.

c_double11.title: Night shifts before Singles' Day or not
c_double11.situation: A month before Singles' Day the factory moves to two shifts, and the night shift's piece rate doubles. On nights you'd have to sleep by day, and the children wouldn't see you when they came home from school; your mother-in-law says she can cope, only her back isn't good.

options.label: Work nights
options.result: You worked a month of nights in a row, eating a bowl of instant noodles in the workshop at three in the morning. After Singles' Day you got the biggest month's pay of your life and bought your mother-in-law a massager.

options.label: Days only
options.result: You still clocked off a little after five and helped the children with their homework in the evening. The women on nights said you'd missed out on thousands; you said children are harder to raise than money is to earn.

c_cert.title: Sit the Level 4 Herbal Tea Processing Worker certificate
c_cert.situation: The city's vocational skills testing station has started an herbal tea processing exam. The factory says anyone with the Level 4 certificate gets ¥200 more a month, and it will count when team leaders are chosen later. The exam means memorizing hygiene rules and processing methods, and you haven't touched a textbook since middle school.

options.label: Sit it
options.result: Every night after the children were asleep you leaned over the dinner table memorizing questions, and your elder child set you tests. The practical was setting up the dryer, and you got it exactly right. You passed.

options.label: Don't
options.result: You said knowing the work in your hands is enough. That evening you watched a cartoon with the children and fell asleep before they did.

c_xiamen.title: Go to Xiamen with your husband
c_xiamen.situation: Your husband has found steady work in Xiamen and wants you there too: a big food factory he knows is hiring and pays thirty percent more than here, and your old electronics factory is hiring as well, saying former staff go straight back in as line leaders. The children could transfer to school in Xiamen, only the rent is high and your mother-in-law won't go.

options.label: Go to the big food factory in Xiamen
options.result: You rented a room off Xiamen island, and the children changed schools. The big factory's workshop is ten times the size of the old one, with ten times the rules, and you started again as a machine operator.

options.label: Go back to the electronics factory as line leader
options.result: You went back to that electronics factory and ran a line of thirty people, facing circuit boards at the stations all day.
options.end: You went back to the electronics factory in Xiamen as a line leader, later a workshop supervisor; passing the tea shelves in the supermarket, you still pick up a pack of chrysanthemum tea to see which factory made it.

options.label: Stay in Longhai
options.result: You said the children had only just settled into school here. Your husband went to Xiamen alone and takes the bullet train home every weekend.

c_leader.title: Apply for Team Leader
c_leader.situation: The team leader who trained you has been moved to the new workshop, and the owner will pick a replacement from the machine operators: assigning a dozen people, every order's progress, spot checks and handovers would all be yours. The other candidate is a distant relative of the owner, who's been at the factory longer than you.

options.label: Apply
options.result: You took the causes of jams and changeover times you'd noted in your little book over the years, put them into a table and gave it to the owner. He had you lead for a month as a trial, and that month your shift's downtime halved.

options.label: Don't apply
options.result: The relative became team leader and still comes to ask you about the machines. You still clock off on time, in time to collect the children.

c_smart_line.title: Learn to tune the new line or not
c_smart_line.situation: The factory is installing a smart line fitted with sensors, where the system sets drying and roasting temperatures and times to the recipe automatically and raises its own alarms. The equipment maker wants a few people to learn to read the data and adjust the parameters; training is in the evenings, and knowing it pays nothing extra.

options.label: Learn it
options.result: In the evenings you listened to the equipment maker's lessons on a tablet and learned to read temperature and humidity curves. Once the line was live, whenever the system alarmed everyone came to fetch you, and one look at the curve told you whether the material was too wet or a probe was dirty.

options.label: Don't
options.result: You said you still trust your hands. You can run the new line, and when it alarms you go and fetch someone from maintenance.

c_shop.title: Open an online shop selling green-herb tea
c_shop.situation: Someone from the village has hit it big online selling southern Fujian green-herb tea. Your cousin says you know the material and the processing, and there are herbs on the hill at home, so why not make a brand of your own: she'll do the livestreams, you'll handle the goods. But a small workshop can't get a food production license, so you'd need a factory to make it.

options.label: Quit and do it
options.result: You had your old factory make it, went up the hill to buy herbs yourself and inspected every delivery yourself, while your cousin talked in the livestream about the bowl of cooling tea you drank as a child. The first year lost money; by the second you had repeat customers.
options.end: You and your cousin built a little brand of southern Fujian green-herb tea, made at your old factory; you go up the hill to look at every batch of herbs yourself before you'll take it.

options.label: Stay at the factory
options.result: You said you still like the workshop. Your cousin later went into business with someone else, and on launch day you bought ten packs and gave them to the women in the workshop.

c_director.title: Workshop Director or not
c_director.situation: The workshop director has retired, and the owner wants you to take over. The director runs the schedule, equipment and hygiene, fronts the brands' audits and complaints, and has to speak at meetings. You only went to middle school, and you still don't know all the English acronyms in the audits.

options.label: Take it
options.result: You bought a book on food safety management and read a few pages every night. The first time you accompanied a brand's audit, you walked from the raw-material store to the finished-goods store and could pull out every record; at the end the auditor said: the floor is well run.

options.label: Recommend someone else
options.result: You recommended a graduate from quality control. He handles the reports and you handle the people in the workshop; at audits he talks through the documents and you lead them round the floor.

c_manager.title: Production Manager or not
c_manager.situation: The factory has added a third workshop, and the owner wants a production manager over the whole place: the production plan, new product samples, equipment purchases and the annual license inspection would all be yours, plus negotiating capacity and delivery dates with the brands. You have ten-odd years left before you retire.

options.label: Take it
options.result: Every day you look at the orders first and the workshops second, and spend half a day on the phone haggling with a brand over a delivery date. On the day the new workshop started up, you were still the first through the air shower.

options.label: Keep your workshop
options.result: You recommended someone from a big factory outside. You still run your workshop, and every morning you stand a while by the sorting table.

endings.retire: On your last day you still got to the factory at quarter to eight, changed, tucked in your hair and stepped into the air shower, counting to ten with your eyes shut. That morning you didn't go to the office; you sat a while by the sorting table and picked over a bowl of chrysanthemum buds, plucking out the black-hearted and the insect-holed one by one. When you clocked off, you left the reading glasses hanging by the sorting table.
endings.burnout: After Singles' Day that year, your back and legs gave out together, and you had to lean on a machine to stand through a morning meeting. You only heard half of what the doctor said. You told the owner you were done. Later, when the old people of the village went up the hill to pick herbs, you followed behind, helping them tell which plant was beggarticks.

stages: Most of your day is at the sorting table: crate after crate of chrysanthemum buds, roses and cassia seeds tipped onto the stainless steel, and you pick the black-hearted, the insect-bored, the stalks and stones into the bowl. In the afternoons you're often moved to the packing line to box, label and pull ten bags to weigh. The women opposite are faster than you, and the team leader comes three times a day to look at the bowl you've picked out.

A pyramid tea-bag packer is yours now: the pre-start check, changing the film roll, setting the weighing to the process sheet, checking weights and seals every half hour, stopping to clear it when it jams. You can cover the dryer and the roaster too, watching the temperature gauge and squeezing a handful of material to feel how dry it is. Your name goes on the machine checklist every day, and every minute it stands idle, the team leader can see.

A shift of a dozen people is yours to lead: you run the pre-shift meeting in the morning, read out today's orders and decide who's on which machine; all day you walk the workshop, watching progress and spot checks and dealing with jams and quality problems; before clocking off you write the handover book. Newcomers learn the machines from you, and when the women have something on at home, they come to you first to swap shifts. You run machines less now, and watch people more.

A workshop is yours to run: the schedule, equipment maintenance and hygiene checks all need your nod. When brands come to audit, you go with them from the raw-material store to the finished-goods store; when complaints come in, you take your people through the records line by line. Every week you meet quality control and purchasing, and when raw material fails, it's your signature on the rejection; people in the workshop still call you big sister out of habit.

All the factory's production is yours: every day you check the order system first, then plan three workshops' schedules; new product samples, equipment purchases and the license's annual inspection are all led by you. When brands want more volume or earlier delivery, you negotiate call by call; when the owner asks whether to take on a new client, you work out the capacity before you answer. Once a week you still go to the sorting table, to look at the bowl of impurities picked out.
work: A crate of rosebuds has a lot of open blooms mixed in, and you pick them out one by one into another bowl. The team leader glances over and says the open ones go for flower tea powder, don't throw them away.

Boxing, you notice the printed production date is smudged on one box's outer bags. You pull them and take them to the operator, who adjusts the ink on the coding printer, and that batch is printed again.
Sorting cassia seeds, you pick out a little stone just as black and just as big as the seeds. Quality control comes to look and says the sorter can't tell those apart; it's down to your hands.

The packer's pyramid bags keep sealing badly. You stop the machine and look for ages, and find a thin layer of sugar dust stuck to the sealing blade. You wipe it clean with an alcohol swab and turn the sealing temperature up five degrees.

The day you cover the dryer, a batch of green herbs comes in especially wet. You dry it for the time on the process sheet, squeeze a handful and it's still soft, so you give it twenty minutes more and test it on the moisture meter until it passes.
Changing the film roll for a new tea, you load it following the manual, and the first bag comes out with the printing upside down. You laugh, take it off and reload it, and the second bag is right.

An order of twenty thousand bags has to ship two days early. You split your shift into three groups on rotation and take a machine yourself. On delivery day you stand at the finished-goods store door and count the last box.

In a spot check, a batch of chrysanthemum and cassia seed is slightly over on moisture. You don't let it into the packing line; you have the dryer run it again, and write in the handover book exactly which batch and by how much.
Two women on your shift start arguing over who gets the easy machine. You don't rule on it; you draw up a rotation chart and pin it on the wall, a week each, so no one loses out.

A big brand comes to audit, and the auditor asks how you handle pest control. You take him to see the number and inspection record on every rodent trap, and the last one, in the furthest corner of the warehouse, you find as well.

Inspecting a delivery of imported roselle, the color looks dull, and the supplier says that's normal. You brew a cup, then brew a cup from last year's retained sample, and set them side by side. The supplier goes quiet.

The workshop's dehumidifier breaks down with the damp season about to arrive. You don't wait for the repair process; you phone the equipment maker directly, and that afternoon someone comes to replace the compressor.

A new client wants half a million bags a month, and the owner asks if you can take it. You spread three workshops' schedules out and work at it all evening, and say yes, but it needs another packing line and ten more people.

For the license's annual inspection, the inspectors spend a morning going through the records. You lay the raw-material intake, test reports and retained-sample logs on the table book by book, and when they leave they raise only one item to fix.

A brand wants a new product, and three rounds of samples come back "not fragrant enough." You take the sample room team to where the raw material is grown, come back and switch to another supplier's dried longan, and at the fourth version the brand signs off.
past: You grew up in a village in Longhai, Zhangzhou, with a grove of longan trees outside the door. In summer, when the heat got into you, your grandmother picked a bunch of herbs on the hill and boiled a pot of bitter cooling tea on the stove, and made you drink a bowl.

After middle school your family couldn't afford to keep two children in high school, and you gave your place to your younger brother. You followed some girls from the village to an electronics factory in Xiamen.
On the line you inserted circuit boards, ten hours a day, with hands among the fastest on the line. The line leader said if you'd had more schooling, you'd have been a team leader long ago.
At the factory you met the man who is now your husband; he worked in the next workshop. You went back to Longhai for the wedding, and the next year your first child came.

When your elder child was due to start kindergarten, your mother-in-law couldn't manage alone, and you quit the electronics factory and went home. Then your second came, and you spent six years raising them.

When the younger one started first grade, you saw a hiring notice at the village entrance for the tea factory on your doorstep: women preferred, lunch provided, close to home. You rode your e-bike to the interview, and HR looked at your hands and said start tomorrow.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Zhangzhou's urban employee pension scheme. You paid in for a few years in Xiamen when you were young, had a six-year gap raising the children, and after joining the factory paid in on the minimum base, so in retirement you get a little over 40% of your last monthly salary.
scenes: Your first week of retirement, at quarter to eight every morning you still freeze for a moment, your hand going to your head to tuck your hair into a cap.

The factory asks you back to train newcomers two mornings a week. You don't talk about rules; you just sit at the sorting table and sort alongside the young newcomers, then go over their bowls once more when they're done.
When your granddaughter comes over after school, you make her a cup of chrysanthemum tea and glance at the manufacturer's address on the bag: the factory where you spent more than twenty years.
For the first few months after leaving the factory you didn't want to do anything. You sat under the longan trees in a daze, listening to the factory's packing machines clacking in the distance.

Once your back was a bit better, you followed the old people of the village up the hill to pick herbs and came back to boil a pot of cooling tea on the stove. The neighbor's child took one sip, stuck out his tongue and ran.

One of the old women from the factory came to see you and said the sorting table is gone now, it's all machines. You asked whether the machines sort it clean. Clean, she said, only sometimes they blow out the good ones too.
For the first month after leaving the tea factory, the smell of chrysanthemum brought back that stainless steel sorting table, and your fingers would move by themselves.
The vocational school girl you trained has become a team leader and sends you a photo: her standing at the packing machine, and on the wall behind her, still, the rotation chart you drew up.
The supermarket shelves are full of wellness teas, and you turn the packs over one by one to see who made them. When you see that familiar address, you buy a pack and take it home.

Lots of tea factories have handed sorting and packing to optical sorters and automatic lines, and drying and roasting follow the curves in the system. But whether a batch of material smells right, whether a bag of tea brews fragrant, still needs someone to lean in and smell.

Your legs cramp every winter, from twenty-odd years on your feet in the workshop. When family come at New Year, you still make everyone a cup of chrysanthemum tea out of habit, picking out the few black-hearted buds first.
Half the longan grove by your door has been cut down for new factory buildings. Walking past with your grandson, you point at one and say: your grandma used to sort flowers in a building like that.

closing.retire: One afternoon many years later, you sit on the balcony making tea for your granddaughter, and before the chrysanthemum goes into the cup you still look over it bud by bud out of habit, and pick out one gone black at the heart.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you sit under the longan trees at the village entrance, and the summer wind carries the bitter smell of cooling tea being boiled. You close your eyes, sniff, and say: there's plantain in that.
closing.end: Many years later, sorting through old things, you find the blue cap the factory gave you, washed almost white. You fold it and put it in the drawer, next to the little notebook of reasons the machine jammed.
